articles.title: Get the lead out: Millions still drink water from contaminated pipes
articles.summary: The solution is clear: Replace the pipes.
articles.body:
Every parent who mixes tap water with baby formula trusts that it is safe. For too many families, that trust depends on pipes made of unknown materials and in uncertain condition.

As the country commemorates National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week , new data serves as a reminder that lead in drinking water remains a serious public health threat — particularly for the approximately 2.17 million people who have elevated lead levels in their drinking water systems. The affected systems span the country, from Illinois and Pennsylvania to Texas and Oregon.

Lead service lines, which connect water mains to homes and other buildings, are a major source of contamination. For children, lead exposure can harm brain development, learning and behavior, with consequences that can last a lifetime. In adults, lead exposure can increase the risk of high blood pressure, kidney damage and reproductive health problems. There is no known safe level of lead exposure.

The solution is clear: Replace the pipes. Communities across the country are making meaningful progress, but sustained investment is needed to ensure every community has the resources to finish the job.

The Trump administration has highlighted its efforts to reduce lead exposure as part of the Environmental Protection Agency’s 100 actions to protect children’s health . These include providing hands-on assistance to more than 100 communities working to remove lead service lines and issuing guidance to help water systems navigate replacement requirements.

Federal funding has also helped communities make meaningful progress.

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act committed $15 billion specifically to lead service line replacement over five years, but estimates place the total cost of replacing the nation’s lead service lines at $50 billion to $80 billion . With at least 4 million lead service lines still in use , the funding gap remains substantial. As dedicated federal funding winds down, communities will face difficult choices. Without additional federal support, more of the financial burden could fall on families to cover replacement costs through higher water bills.

The EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements , finalized in October 2024, set a 10-year replacement timeline for most water systems. Meeting that deadline requires identifying pipes, planning projects, coordinating with property owners and carrying out construction — all of which take money and time.

Lead-pipe replacement also delivers benefits beyond safer drinking water. Research from Michigan cited in a recent white paper estimated $3.24 billion in future benefits from replacing lead service lines, including reduced lead exposure for more than 420,000 newborns. Preventing exposure can help spare children and communities the lasting consequences of lead’s effects on development and learning.

Families also need protection while they wait for lead pipes to be replaced. Because replacement work can temporarily increase lead levels in drinking water, certified lead-reducing filters can help limit exposure in the meantime.

Congress can build on the progress already made by funding three priorities in the next appropriations cycle. It is incumbent upon lawmakers to provide additional funding to the Drinking Water State Revolving Loan Fund , the Reducing Lead in Drinking Water Program , and the Voluntary School and Child Care Lead Testing and Reduction Program . Lawmakers should also advance proposals to expand access to certified point-of-use filtration in schools and child care facilities and establish a new federal filtration pilot program to protect families while permanent infrastructure improvements are underway.

These investments would help communities replace pipes, identify and address contamination, and protect children where they learn and spend their days. They would also reinforce efforts already underway at the federal, state and local levels.

National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week is an opportunity to raise awareness, but awareness must lead to action. The EPA has provided funding, technical assistance and practical guidance. Congress and the administration must ensure communities have the resources to finish the job.

Parents across the country want confidence that the water coming from their kitchen taps will not harm their children. Reducing lead exposure requires a combination of immediate protections and long-term infrastructure improvements. The country has made meaningful progress, but completing the work will require sustained investment.

Every child deserves safe drinking water, and every community should have a fair chance to deliver it.

Mae Stevens is executive director of the Protect Kids From Lead Coalition.

articles.title: Trump administration: Hundreds of Washington state voters may be noncitizens
articles.summary: Federal officials on Monday called on Washington state’s election officials to set aside ballots from over 400 people they say have illegally registered to vote without U.S. citizenship. The Justice Department (DOJ), in a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, said it has identified 1,500 votes cast by the more than 400 people…
articles.body:
Federal officials on Monday called on Washington state’s election officials to set aside ballots from over 400 people they say have illegally registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.

The Justice Department (DOJ), in a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, said it has identified 1,500 votes cast by the more than 400 people in prior elections, the Associated Press reported . The department asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in the upcoming midterm elections until state officials can confirm their eligibility to vote.

“For years Washington State has had a mantra: our elections are ‘free, fair, and devoid of fraud.’ But our investigation shows not all of that is true – people who are non-citizens are registered to vote and are voting in our state,” Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, wrote in a press release Monday.

Floyd called the over 400 noncitizens identified by the department “only the tip of the iceberg.”

Hobbs said he was reviewing the DOJ’s request with his office, noting that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted, according to the AP report.

“The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Hobbs said in the AP report.

According to the DOJ release, many of the people in the list are lawful permanent residents or “green card” holders who, the department notes, have legal immigration status but are not allowed to vote in U.S. elections.

Federal law dictates that only U.S. citizens are permitted to vote in federal elections, according to a fact sheet from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The DOJ released notes that if a noncitizen is registered to vote, they should report that to the Secretary of State’s Office to cancel their registration.

“We have heard from green card holders who were registered against their knowledge via the Washington Motor Voter program,” the release said. “Then they receive a ballot in the mail and assume they are legally registered – that simply is not the case.”

The move, which comes roughly a week before the midterm elections, is the latest effort by the Trump administration in identifying noncitizen voters.

Last week, the DOJ charged 28 California voters who are allegedly not U.S. citizens in criminal complaints with federal crimes. All 28 individuals are lawful permanent residents some of whom, the department said , fraudulently registered to vote in U.S. elections.

Earlier this month, the department sued California , after giving it a USB drive and demanding that within 48 hours the state compare 20,000 names on its data rolls with information provided by the Department of Homeland Security.

articles.title: Supporting religious freedom and pluralism is a foreign policy priority
articles.summary: A country that protects its pluralism and presses its partners to protect theirs is not only living its ideals; it is protecting its future.
articles.body:
Each year on Oct. 27, the U.S. marks International Religious Freedom Day, the anniversary of the 1998 law that made defending conscience abroad a standing aim of American foreign policy. The observance is best understood as a statement about what keeps a country stable, ours included.

The principle behind International Religious Freedom Day is straightforward. A nation’s strength is enhanced when neighbors from different faith traditions can rely upon and trust one another. The founders wagered that a multiplicity of faiths, where all are free to exercise their faith, would yield stability rather than chaos.

We have not always kept that promise. In the Blaine Amendment era, states wrote bans on aid to “sectarian” schools into their constitutions — restrictions widely understood as targeting Catholic schools. Jewish Americans have experienced a sharp rise in antisemitic incidents since Oct. 7, 2023.

Black churches have been targeted by racists for generations, from the 1963 Birmingham bombing that killed four girls to the 2015 murders at Emanuel AME in Charleston. In the aftermath of 9/11, Muslims and Arabs endured hate crimes. Each time, we were weaker for it.

That is why Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s travels matter. His commitment to religious freedom long predates his tenure at State. As a senator, he supported bipartisan measures, including the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act and reauthorization of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom.

Earlier this month, he was in India, where proposed amendments to a foreign contribution law would let authorities revoke a charity’s license over vague concerns about social or religious harmony, then take control of its assets. Many of the schools, hospitals and orphanages at stake trace back to missionaries such as Saint Francis Xavier. The bill has been paused and sent to a parliamentary committee, but it has not been withdrawn.

A sovereign nation may regulate foreign money. It should not give officials a vague standard and the power to seize a church’s property.

The administration has also nominated Jane “Cissie” Graham Lynch as ambassador at large for international religious freedom. The daughter of Evangelical pastor Franklin Graham, Lynch has worked with the relief organization Samaritan’s Purse since 2010. She was also appointed as a non-voting member of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, a commission now at full strength.

Last month, President Trump also appointed Catholic Bishop Robert Barron, former White House domestic policy chief Joe Grogan, and Pastor Andrew Brunson, who was imprisoned in Turkey. They joined six commissioners chosen by congressional leaders of both parties.

Lynch’s confirmation should restore something the law already requires. The International Religious Freedom Act directs the ambassador to report directly to the secretary of State; a requirement Rubio helped write into law as a cosponsor of the 2016 amendments. Recent reorganization has blurred that line by realigning the office under the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor. A confirmed ambassador with direct access to the secretary can carry the cause of the persecuted to the one official who can act.

That American commitment has a global resonance. Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, has pressed the case for peace persistently. Within days of his election, he offered the Vatican as a mediator, insisting war is never inevitable. To warring leaders, he pleaded , “Let us meet, let us talk, let us negotiate!” He has named hotspots of religious persecution and brought representatives of the world’s major religions together in an appeal for peace .

Peace is not passivity. Aggressors must be stopped, the vulnerable defended and the guilty held accountable. Civil authority must also step in when religion is misappropriated to subjugate or harm others. Faith invoked as cover for violence, coercion or abuse is not religious freedom but its counterfeit. Free societies must draw that line carefully and evenly.

Blessed are the peacemakers. A country that protects its pluralism and presses its partners to protect theirs is not only living its ideals; it is protecting its future.

Andrea Picciotti-Bayer is director of the Conscience Project.

articles.title: FBI raids California home tied to former Congressman Eric Swalwell - US media
articles.summary: The California Democrat has faced multiple sexual misconduct allegations which he has denied.
articles.body:
FBI officers raided a California home in connection with the investigation into former US Congressman Eric Swalwell, US media reports.

Swalwell, 45, dropped out of California's governor's race earlier this year and gave up his seat in the House of Representatives after allegations of sexual misconduct while in office emerged.

In August, the FBI stopped the former Democratic lawmaker at an airport, seized his electronic devices and raided his Washington DC home as part of the investigation into those allegations.

Swalwell has in the past denied any wrongdoing and his attorney has called them "fabricated".

"These accusations are false, fabricated, and deeply offensive - a calculated and transparent political hit job," his attorney Sara Azari said around the time they were first reported.

The BBC has contacted Swalwell's lawyer for comment.

In statements, the justice department and FBI said only that "early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment."

The enforcement action took place at a house in Beverly Hills, a source familiar with the inquiry confirmed to the BBC.

Public records indicate the address was associated with Stephen Cloobeck, a billionaire and former California gubernatorial candidate who had once backed Swalwell's campaign for governor.

Swalwell had stayed at the home previously, the Los Angeles Times reported.

An attorney for Cloobeck did not immediately provide comment to the BBC.

In an April interview with the New York Post, Cloobeck said he had stopped supporting Swalwell after multiple women accused the former lawmaker of misconduct.

Swalwell has faced allegations from multiple women, including that he raped one victim while she was too intoxicated to respond and that he sent women unsolicited nude photographs. He is also facing separate probes in New York City and Los Angeles regarding the allegations. Swalwell has denied the allegations and has never been criminally charged.

Once a high-profile Democrat that had become a fixture of cable news shows criticising President Donald Trump - and briefly considered a likely future governor of California - Swalwell was abruptly forced to end his gubernatorial bid after the allegations surfaced.

The House ethics committee also began investigating, but stopped once Swalwell left Congress.

Additionally, the White House in August declassified documents from a separate, unrelated FBI investigation into his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Many of those details regarding his 2015 relationship with Christine Fang were already known, and he never faced any related charges.

articles.title: Sophia Bush opens up on midterms, her new book — and why she won’t say Trump’s name
articles.summary: Don’t count Sophia Bush among the performers who plan on stepping back from making their voices heard in the political world. “What would I do? Silence myself? Take away one of my most important rights to be more palatable or more hirable to people I don’t know? That’s not something that I’m interested in,” Bush…
articles.body:
Don’t count Sophia Bush among the performers who plan on stepping back from making their voices heard in the political world.

“What would I do? Silence myself? Take away one of my most important rights to be more palatable or more hirable to people I don’t know? That’s not something that I’m interested in,” Bush said in a recent interview with ITK , when asked if it was a tough choice to decide whether to get involved in politics back in 2008 when she campaigned for then-Democratic presidential nominee Sen. Barack Obama (Ill.).

“If anything, I think that my ability to have had these experiences, to be out on the campaign trail, to see myself in all of my neighbors — whether they’re in small town Texas or northern Vermont or the center of Los Angeles — is something that makes me a better advocate, but it also makes me a better actor,” the 44-year-old “Work in Progress” podcast host said.

“I connect with people in a very real way and feel like I can tell their stories no matter where they’re from. And the only way I can do that is actually by showing up somewhere to advocate and then listening to them, listening to their stories, listening to their experiences, understanding what their pain points are, what they need from this country that they’re not getting and that they clearly deserve,” she said.

The former “One Tree Hill” and “Chicago P.D.” star opened up about life in both the entertainment and political spotlight in a wide-ranging conversation about her new book, “And I Will Tell You Mine.”

“You have stories you’re finally ready to tell, and I think for me, after years of advocating for other people and for community, it felt really special to turn that patient attention inward and actually decide to share some things about my own personal individual life,” Bush said of her first foray into literature.

The book details her upbringing in Los Angeles and how she begrudgingly fell in love with acting while a student at the University of Southern California, switching from its journalism school to its theater program. Much like acting, she writes in the book, activism “truly felt like a calling.”

One chapter in “And I Will Tell You Mine: Notes from a Life in Progress,” titled “The Last Dance Party,” describes Bush’s mad dash to get to a final, star-studded bash during President Obama’s second term in the White House in 2017.

Bush said she had missed an email about a “sort of last hurrah” at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave., before receiving a call from one of her friends in the Obama administration about the farewell fete that night.

“I wound up rerouting my flight and getting to D.C. and landing in sweatpants and having to figure out how to scramble a White House appropriate outfit,” Bush recalled. The entertainer made a frantic stop at a Saks Off 5th outlet store: “They’d have something, and it would be on sale. Win-win,” she wrote.

While the chapter focuses on what Bush called “one of the most beautiful, memorable evenings,” it also strikes a critical tone about President Trump.

“Despite running the most qualified person for president to date, misogyny had prevailed at the end of 2016,” Bush said of Trump’s win in the White House race against Hillary Clinton. Without mentioning the president by name, Bush said Trump had “won on bluster and wildly crass tendencies.”

“I think someone who chooses to exemplify and bolster the very worst of human tendency doesn’t really deserve to have their name spoken,” Bush said.

“It’s the same reason that I think it’s incredibly important to speak the names of school children that are lost in school shootings, and not the name of the school shooter. When you are wreaking terror on a community, I don’t think you deserve to be a star,” she said.

Saying Trump “has made things so much worse for women in the last 10 years,” Bush told ITK, “I know we’re fed up, and I know plenty of men are fed up, too. And it’s about time that we take the nation back and choose to elect leaders that might not own people in a tweet but get the job done.”

“It’s absolutely abhorrent what’s happening in our country, in our economy, and in our culture right now because of that man’s leadership, so no, I’m not particularly interested in saying his name. But I’ll be one of the voices that continues to call out his bad actions until he’s out of office proudly, because I love my country.”

Asked about the 2028 White House race, Bush said she’s laser focused on the midterm elections, expressing optimism about Democratic candidates’ chances across the country.

“I think the midterms are really an opportunity for us to leave it all on the field and hopefully claw back some of the democracy that our great republic is meant to operate with and signify in the world.”

“I think if we’re just going on the numbers, on American sentiment and on the reality that’s hit so many people, we should see greater than a blue wave — we should see a blue landslide,” Bush said.

While some performers have questioned whether they want to continue speaking out about politics — following former Vice President Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential election loss, “The Hunger Games” actor Jennifer Lawrence wondered aloud in an interview with The New York Times whether she was adding “fuel to a fire that’s ripping the country apart” by sharing her opinion — Bush indicated that she has no intention of silencing herself.

“I think it’s wild to tell any citizen that they should just stick to their job rather than love their country,” she said.

“Every single person who lives in this country has as much a right to stand up for it as anyone else,” Bush said, adding that she didn’t want to compare herself to or judge other people in the industry for their personal choices and her peers’ “very valid feelings around those things.”

“For me, I don’t think celebrity activism matters. I don’t even like the word celebrity,” Bush continued.

“But what I do think is that when someone you know cares enough about something to have a conversation with you, it can move the needle. And I care about this stuff.”

“I don’t show up to advocate because it might be good for my job,” Bush said.

“If anything, being a quiet mystery who nobody can identify with an opinion might be better for my job as an actor — but it’s just not the way I choose to live life.”

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy, have you no sense of decency?
articles.summary: Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy faced widespread condemnation from both Democrats and fellow Republicans for releasing a television advertisement featuring the mother of Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton, a move that critics compared to the unethical tactics of Sen. Joseph McCarthy.
articles.body:
One thing for sure about politics these days. Just when you think political rhetoric could sink no lower, some candidate takes things to a new low. This week, the all-time, cringeworthy, I-can’t-believe-he-would-actually-say-that award goes to Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy.

It didn’t used to be that way. I’ve been a political junkie since 1968, when I first walked through the doors of a campaign office: in San Francisco, for presidential candidate Sen. Eugene McCarthy (D-Minn.).

Two things I learned early on about politics. One, it’s important. It’s about more than winning elections. It’s about deciding what kind of city, state or country we want, what kind of people we are and whom we want to represent us.

Two, even though politics is hardball and not beanbag, there was still some sense of civility. You could disagree with your opponent strongly, but you never lied, never engaged in personal insults, and never attacked members of an opponent’s family.

All that changed, of course, with President Trump, who broke all the rules. He insulted fellow Republican candidates: “Little Marco” Rubio; “Lyin’ Ted” Cruz; “Low Energy” Jeb Bush. He lied about winning the popular vote in 2016 . He accused former President Barack Obama of “treason” for “rigging” the 2016 and 2020 elections.

There’s hardly a Democratic or Republican critic of his that Trump hasn’t insulted, ridiculed or lied about. Under his brand of politics, there is no bottom anymore. No matter how disgusting, anything goes. And nobody has embraced Trump’s race to the gutter more than Vivek Ramaswamy.

In a new low for politics, Ramaswamy released a television ad last week in which Donna Arthur, mother of Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton, looks into the camera and tells voters: “Don’t let her become your governor. … She is a liar.”

Parachuting his opponent’s mother into the governor’s race is wrong enough, but the nature of the relationship between Acton and her mother makes Ramaswamy’s ad truly despicable.

Arthur lost custody of Acton and her brother after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton. There’s no dispute about the facts. According to police and court documents, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter , then 12, in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.

State authorities removed Acton and her brother from their home and placed them in foster care. Acton has not spoken to her mother since, in roughly 50 years.

Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury in September 1978, but failed to show at a court hearing . Acton’s mother stayed with her husband and helped him escape law enforcement authorities until he died in 2004.

As a sign there’s still some decency left in politics, Ramaswamy’s decision to exploit a family’s tragic history and present a woman who sided with her daughter’s rapist as a spokesperson for his campaign even offended his fellow Ohio Republicans. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) said Ramaswamy should take down the ad. Sen. John Husted (R-Ohio), running for reelection, and Secretary of State Frank LaRose (R) also condemned the ad .

In fact, many Republicans were outraged by Ramaswamy’s “mommy liar” ad. But not JD Vance. And not Trump.

Vance, who recently wrote a book celebrating his conversion to Catholicism, told Republicans to “stop whining.” Instead, he said, we should thank Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is.”

For his part, Trump praised the ad, saying it was like “ hitting pay dirt .” He not only liked the ad, he said he was jealous about it. He told an Iowa campaign rally: “ I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody .”

Watching Ramaswamy, Vance and Trump wallow in the dirt recalls that historic moment in the Army-McCarthy hearings of 1954 , where attorney Joseph Welch served as chief counsel for the U.S. Army against Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s (R-Wis.) charges that the Pentagon was riddled with communists.

When McCarthy also accused a young member of Welch’s law firm of being a communist, Welch asked the famous question that ended McCarthy’s career and still echoes today: “Have you no sense of decency, sir?”

No, Joseph McCarthy had no sense of decency then. And neither does Ramaswamy, Vance or Trump today.

articles.title: The ‘weapon of war’ argument has backfired on AR-15 bans
articles.summary: The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County regarding the constitutionality of state and local bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles.
articles.body:
The Supreme Court will soon hear arguments in December in Viramontes v. Cook County , a challenge to state and local bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. The challengers say the rifles are “in common use” for lawful purposes such as self-defense. The state governments defending their gun-bans say they are weapons better suited to war than to civilian life.

Neither side recognizes that the Second Amendment’s reference to the “militia” counts in favor of protecting AR-15s either way.

The challengers emphasize self-defense, an individually focused concern, while the governments argue that AR-15s’ military character is a reason to ban them. But AR-15s are the sort of small arms historically suited for a militia. This is actually the heart of the case, as we argued in a friend-of-the-court brief for the Cato Institute.

Small arms that an infantryman would historically have kept and borne are not marginal to the Second Amendment. Rather, they sit at its center. The amendment’s self-professed rationale for protecting the right to keep and bear arms is that a well-regulated militia is necessary to the security of a free state.

Although self-defense is also an important aspect of the right, debates about how useful AR-15s are for that purpose as compared to, say, pistols — or about how useful they are on a modern battlefield versus against a nighttime home intruder — miss the point.

The Second Amendment’s own text says it is protecting an individual right out of a recognition of the militia’s importance. The provision reads: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.”

The Second Amendment is unique in spelling out both a social purpose and an individual protection. Advocates for gun-control have long argued that the purpose cabins the protection, such that the Second Amendment protects only “the right of the people of each of the several States to maintain a well-regulated militia,” in the words of Justice John Paul Stevens’s dissent from the landmark case District of Columbia v. Heller .

Stevens had a point in taking the amendment’s reference to the militia seriously. But the majority of his colleagues better understood what it means. In an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, they observed that historically, the militia referred to “all able-bodied men,” who would be called into duty by the government in emergency situations.

Further, the term “free State” meant “a free polity,” not the specific state governments existing within the United States. The Second Amendment’s Framers deemed an armed population a safeguard for a free society. The militia, writ large, would be “useful in repelling invasions and suppressing insurrections.” It would discourage the establishment of “large standing armies” that could threaten republican liberty. And if need be, a public “trained in arms and organized” would be “better able to resist tyranny.”

This last aim, enabling resistance to tyranny, deserves particular emphasis. The “people’s militia” could fight a tyrant and thus defend freedom. A militia controlled exclusively by the government could not. The Second Amendment guarantees an individual right for more than just individually focused purposes.

It is possible to overread the prefatory clause, and the Heller majority takes care to note that the Second Amendment does not cover dangerous and unusual weapons, nor does it guarantee that the general populace will be able to effectively fight against a modern military. The court also anticipated an objection: If “weapons that are most useful in military service — M-16 rifles and the like — may be banned, then the Second Amendment right is completely detached from the prefatory clause.” The governments in the Viramontes ruling agree.

The historical context of the Second Amendment’s reference to the militia provides the answer. At the time the Bill of Rights was enacted, men were expected to keep small arms suited to infantry service and bear them when summoned for militia duty. They were not expected to lug around artillery, much less to show up at muster with crew-manned weaponry. The AR-15, a readily portable semiautomatic rifle (indeed, this is a major feature distinguishing AR-15s from M-16s, which are capable of fully automatic fire), sits neatly within the class of arms a militia member held historically. Far from being a fatal strike against its constitutional protection, that weighs in its favor.

In deciding Viramontes,the court should decline the invitation to build an ahistorical wall between guns for self-defense that enjoy protection and what some courts call “weapons of war” that lack it.

Matthew Cavedon is the director of the Cato Institute’s Project on Criminal Justice.

articles.title: Trump doubles down in Texas
articles.summary: Plus: 🍻Brewers one win away from first World Series title {beacon} It’s Tuesday. We’re a week out from Election Day. In today’s issue: Double dose of Trump in Texas Debate in the Hawkeye State DOJ, California tussle over ballots East Potomac Park fight Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. We’re a week out from Election Day.

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

President Trump is set to make not one, but two stops in Texas on Tuesday, scheduled to appear at 3 p.m. EDT in Corpus Christi and at 7 p.m. in Lubbock.

Trump’s two events in the Lone Star State in one day come exactly a week away from state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) highly contested Senate match against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico .

The president is rallying for Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in his reelection campaign against Democrat Gina Hinojosa .

Senate race continues to shift: Talarico or Paxton will succeed Sen. John Cornyn (R), who lost in the state’s GOP primary after Trump backed the state attorney general.

The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) currently has the state listed as a “toss up,” with Talarico having 57 percent odds to win compared to Paxton’s 43 percent.

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report also has the race listed as a “toss up,” having shifted it from “lean Republican” at the end of August.

Talarico has attempted to debate Paxton , who has continuously ignored the offers, the Democrat told TMZ in an interview.

“Ken Paxton has refused to debate and that’s pretty low-T behavior in my book,” Talarico said last week, referring to Paxton’s “Low-T Talarico” insult on his masculinity in a campaign ad.

Trump has blamed the tightened Senate race on Cornyn and GOP strategist Karl Rove due to their lack of support for the Texas attorney general.

Texas House races tighten up : The Senate race won’t be the only interesting match-up to watch next Tuesday in Texas, as several House races have inched closer in polling numbers.

Texas’s 15th and 34th congressional districts border Corpus Christi, and Trump will look to get Republicans from those districts to the polls to help decide those races.

The15th Congressional District — a tall, skinny strip that goes as far north as the San Antonio metro and as far south as the Mexico border — features a close race between Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R) and Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido .

Pulido currently has a 46 percent chance to win, compared to De La Cruz’s 54 percent odds, according to DDHQ, and has pushed the district to be listed as a “toss up.”

The 34th Congressional District “leans Democrat,” according to DDHQ, which lists incumbent Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D) as leading GOP challenger Eric Flores .

Iowa has become one of the closest watched states in the weeks ahead of midterms for its highly contested races in the upper chamber and for governor.

State Auditor Rob Sand (D) and Republican businessperson Zach Lahn (R) will face off in another debate tonight as the two gubernatorial candidates look to make one final push ahead of Election Day.

The winner of next week’s election will succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds (R).

What went down in Round 1?: The two candidates have consistently traded blows over their family backgrounds, with Sand going after Lahn over his ties to Kansas.

“You literally voted in Kansas in 2018 and in ’20 and in ’22. You registered to vote in Iowa less than two years ago,” Sand said to Lahn. “This is not about why you’re in Kansas. This is about the fact that you’re not in Iowa.”

Lahn has defended his travel between the Sunflower and Hawkeye states, saying that he has a blended family, with children living in both states.

The GOP candidate also accused Sand of promoting gender ideology and transgender issues.

According to The Hill’s Caroline Vakil, Sand has mentioned he doesn’t believe transgender women and girls should be playing in women’s sports leagues. But Sand objected to a 2025 law that removed gender identity from the Iowa Civil Rights Code.

What the numbers show: According to a poll from Emerson College Polling and The Hill, Sand has a narrow lead over Lahn.

Forty-nine percent said they supported Sand , while 45 percent favored Lahn. Six percent said they were undecided.

American farmers, who are frustrated by higher production and diesel costs, might pose an unexpected problem for Republicans on Nov. 3.

As The Hill’s Mallory Wilson writes, “Trump won 69 percent of the rural vote in 2024, but recent polls have shown that the voting group is not happy with how it has fared under Trump since the election.”

Recent polling from KFF/AP found that 6 in 10 rural voters disapprove of the president’s management of the economy and cite cost of living as their top issue heading into the midterms.

Farmers have been hit particularly hard by higher diesel prices amid the ongoing war in Iran, perhaps explaining tighter than expected races in states like Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska.

In an April survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation, 94 percent of farmers reported worsening financial circumstances.

“I think that farmers are pretty ticked off,” former Minnesota Republican Senate Majority Leader Amy Frederiksen said.

Not going blue: “They want to vote for Republicans, but this is their business, these are their families, and it doesn’t appear that anyone’s listening,” she added.

A federal appeals court on Monday blocked the Trump administration from ordering California to refuse to count 20,000 mail-in ballots it says are from likely noncitizen voters.

“The United States’s claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,” the court wrote in its decision.

The Department of Justice was seeking to hurry the ruling before the case reached a trial judge. But judges in a 2-1 vote at a rare Sunday hearing were skeptical.

“I don’t see how we have jurisdiction,” U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said in response to the request.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, who was appointed by former President Clinton , will review the case on Tuesday afternoon.

Retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) on Monday expressed concern that Trump is “laying the groundwork” for Republicans to “steal” her state’s Senate election.

In a Monday evening post on the social platform X , Smith wrote, “He’s blatantly laying the groundwork to steal an election if his chosen candidate doesn’t win… Minnesota will not take kindly to thinly veiled threats from a guy we’ve rejected three times (soon to be four).”

Her post was in response to a Truth Social post from the president, endorsing GOP candidate Michele Tafoya .

Was that a threat? Trump added that the “Federal Government will be watching closely” and the “only way [Tafoya] can lose is if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in.”

Recent polling reveals a tight race between Tafoya and her Democratic opponent, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan .

Cook Political Report recently moved its projection from “likely” to “lean” Democratic.

A federal judge on Monday blocked the president from cutting down more trees at the East Potomac Park, where Trump plans to build a new golf course.

“Without meaningful notice to Plaintiffs or the Court, on October 10, it bulldozed hundreds of trees on the Course. It did so even though, as two [National Park Service] officials have testified, there was no urgency,” said U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said.

The order extends a previous decision to a lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League against the White House.

Are you listening? Reyes scolded the Trump administration earlier this month, claiming its lawyers did not give sufficient notice for tree-cutting.

“I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” Reyes said during an emergency hearing. She added that the administration lost “all of its credibility” regarding this case.

Trump isn’t budging: Despite Monday’s ruling, the president said in a Truth Social post on Monday night that “we are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled.”

He went on to say that Reyes “does not have the Constitutional Right to ‘ask for or receive notices,’ which are time-consuming, unnecessary, expensive, and unconstitutional.”

“We will immediately appeal this decision,” Trump continued. “When completed, it is anticipated that this Course, which will be open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C., will be one of the finest anywhere in the World.”

❌The localized ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine brokered by first lady Melania Trump took effect Tuesday. It was announced last week that the first lady secured a temporary humanitarian agreement in the city of Oleshky, Ukraine, which borders Russia.

🎸Singer Neil Young is suing President Trump for using his song “Rockin’ in the Free World” at his Ohio rally — claiming the president’s fundraising team broke a vow made by the two parties. Young is now filing a $10 million copyright infringement lawsuit.

🩺Late Monday night, Trump announced a $250 million initiative to recruit and retain nursing home nurses. The initiative will be under the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

🍁Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday night that trade talks with the U.S. have picked up slightly ahead of midterms. He noted that any progress is “because the U.S. is coming closer to our position.”

articles.title: North Carolina state Senate candidate arrested after police standoff
articles.summary: A North Carolina state Senate candidate was arrested Monday after an hours-long standoff with police, which he detailed as it was happening in a series of posts to social platform X. Jonathan D. Miller, a Libertarian running to represent North Carolina State Senate District 16, was arrested at about 3 p.m. after the standoff, which…
articles.body:
A North Carolina state Senate candidate was arrested Monday after an hours-long standoff with police, which he detailed as it was happening in a series of posts to social platform X .

Jonathan D. Miller, a Libertarian running to represent North Carolina State Senate District 16, was arrested at about 3 p.m. after the standoff, which occurred at his apartment complex near the Lochmere neighborhood in Cary, N.C., according to local news station WRAL .

“The whole police department is chasing me with guns drawn. This should be fun,” Miller said in a morning X post .

“I’ve got six shots and the high ground. I hope they don’t find me, but if they do it’s going to be a hell of a show,” the candidate followed with a comment on the post.

The Cary Police Department said officers conducted a welfare check at about 8:26 a.m. at Miller’s home, WRAL reported. At a Monday news conference, police chief Terry Sult said when authorities found Miller, “he had a firearm and was ordered not to touch it, and he took off running.”

Authorities said Miller is facing charges of communicating threats, resisting officers and going armed to the terror of the public, WRAL reported. The candidate’s court appearance is scheduled for 1:30 p.m. Tuesday in Wake County, N.C.

Authorities said no one was injured in the standoff. Miller reportedly made several calls to WRAL while he was standing off with police, telling the outlet he had posted a suicide note to social media the night prior which had “gone super viral.”

Miller is running against incumbent state Sen. Gale Adcock (D) and Republican Philip Hensley.

articles.body:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reportedly searched a California home tied to its current investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.).

The Beverly Hills mansion, owned by a donor of Swalwell’s, was searched as part of the probe into the former lawmaker, CNN reported , citing two people familiar with the investigation.

“Early this morning the FBI conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment,” the FBI told The Hill on Tuesday.

Swalwell resigned from Congress and terminated his bid for California’s open gubernatorial seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct.

The San Francisco Chronicle published accusations from a former aide that Swalwell sexually assaulted her on two occasions. CNN similarly went live with allegations from three other women making separate accusations of sexual misconduct.

Though Swalwell denied the allegations, a number of notable Democrats dropped their support for his gubernatorial bid, forcing him to quit the race.

Following his resignation from the House, the Department of Justice, along with district attorneys for Los Angeles and Manhattan, launched individual probes into the allegations.

Federal agents have already seized electronics from Swalwell at San Francisco International Airport in August before raiding his Washington, D.C., home the following day as part of the ongoing probe into his sexual assault allegations.

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman previously told The Hill that his office’s Sex Crimes Division is working closely with law enforcement partners “as this investigation unfolds.”

Swalwell is also under investigation by other California state officials for allegations he improperly used campaign finances to pay legal expenses to Los Angeles attorney Sara Azari.

articles.title: Trump says he will respect midterm results ‘if they’re honest elections’
articles.summary: President Trump said on Tuesday that he will respect next week’s midterm results “if they’re honest elections” amid growing concerns from Democrats over his pre-election rhetoric. Trump made the comments at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a campaign trip to Texas. On Monday, Trump warned in a TruthSocial post that he is “watching closely”…
articles.body:
President Trump said on Tuesday that he will respect next week’s midterm results “if they’re honest elections” amid growing concerns from Democrats over his pre-election rhetoric.

Trump made the comments at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a campaign trip to Texas.

On Monday, Trump warned in a TruthSocial post that he is “watching closely” for voter fraud in Minnesota’s Senate race, which has become one of the more competitive races of the cycle.

“Let’s all get behind Michele Tafoya in Minnesota. She’s running a great race. Don’t allow them to play with the Votes after the race is over,” Trump wrote. “The Federal Government will be watching closely.”

“The only way she can lose is if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in,” he added.

The comment was met with swift backlash from Minnesota Democrats, including Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.), who accused the president of “laying the groundwork” to “steal” the election.

“He’s blatantly laying the groundwork to steal an election if his chosen candidate doesn’t win… Minnesota will not take kindly to thinly veiled threats from a guy we’ve rejected three times (soon to be four),” Smith posted on the social platform X.

Meanwhile, over the weekend, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit saying it would block the results of Alaska’s Senate race if incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) loses his reelection bid, accusing another candidate in the race — Dan J. Sullivan — of running to intentionally confuse voters.

Attorney General Todd Blanche vehemently defended the lawsuit during a contentious interview on CNN on Sunday.

“What he [Trump] has said repeatedly, repeatedly, is that the reason why this is not fair — this is not a fair fight in his mind — is because there is a man on the ballot with the same name as the incumbent senator, who happens to be a Republican,” Blanche told the network.

“There could be a crime. But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard,” he said.

articles.title: Justice for Camp Lejeune families cannot depend on an election
articles.summary: Rep. Mark Takano criticized President Donald Trump for suggesting that the settlement of Camp Lejeune veterans’ toxic exposure claims could depend on the outcome of the midterm elections.
articles.body:
“If the Republicans don’t do well, maybe they won’t get their money.” Those are the words of President Trump when asked whether he is tying veterans’ toxic exposure claims to the midterm election results.

Trump stated several times last week that Camp Lejeune veterans with pending claims won’t receive the settlements to which they are entitled if Republicans don’t win the midterms. This is an outrageous breach of trust and a break from accepted norms, and seemingly just another day in this administration.

Democrats included The Camp Lejeune Justice Act in the PACT Act, the largest expansion of veterans’ benefits in history. I authored that bill as chairman of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee, and President Biden signed it into law in 2022 . Including this provision was important because veterans and their families have been waiting decades for relief.

Congress gave these families a legal right to compensation. How fast the Department of Justice settles those claims is an administrative choice, and the president is now suggesting that choice depends on how his party does in November.

There are more than 500,000 claims awaiting relief after decades of injustice. Each claim represents a former servicemember, family member or civilian who was stationed at Camp Lejeune and has suffered serious medical complications from contaminated water.

These are veterans who have battled cancer, serious liver and kidney issues, and other diseases caused by toxic water on base. People have waited years to be made whole and for our country to live up to its promise of taking care of those who serve. They should not be politically blackmailed by a president who has directed the largest cuts to the Department of Veterans Affairs workforce and services in history.

I have led the charge this year to live up to the promise we make to veterans by fighting attempts in Congress to cut future benefits for servicemembers fighting in Iran and by cracking down on billions of dollars going to Trump allies instead of veteran care.

Veterans fought for a country where they could expect their government not to use their benefits as a bargaining chip. Empty promises have been the hallmark of this Congress and this administration — which has passed the lowest number of veteran bills in recent memory. This latest attempt to coerce voters will be rejected by veterans who have served and fought for justice.

If the president were at all concerned with expanding benefits, he would call on Republicans to end their hold on the Major Richard Star Act . When we return to Washington, the House will vote on this critical piece of legislation to end the wounded warrior tax so that our combat-injured veterans can live with dignity.

That is a promise I can get behind: finally delivering the benefits for which 59,000 combat-injured veterans have fought. Instead, we get hollow promises and unmistakable threats to veterans’ benefits, all of which, according to President Trump, hinge on the midterm election results.

Our requirement to care for veterans after their service is a sacred obligation that our government must fulfill. So, I am disappointed although not surprised that Republicans who claim to share this belief have remained silent in the face of this latest attempt to swipe away benefits.

Veterans deserve leaders in Congress who are not afraid to condemn threats from the president and who always stand up for survivors of Camp Lejeune, other veterans exposed to toxic substances, or any former servicemember waiting for justice.

Veterans fought, served, and died for our country — with many still living the impacts of their service. Veterans and their benefits should not be threatened by a man who is more interested in staying in power and avoiding accountability than in delivering for those who selflessly served our nation in uniform.

Mark Takano represents California’s 39th District in the U.S. House of Representatives and is ranking member on the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee.

articles.title: Haley Stevens slams Cenk Uygur’s anti-Israel ad: ‘Fearmongering’
articles.summary: A new political ad put out by Cenk Uygur’s Rebellion PAC really rubs me the wrong way
articles.body:
Like many Americans, I am skeptical of U.S. military aid to Israel, for no other reason than I generally don’t think we should pay for another nation’s security. I’m happy to sell them weapons to fight terrorists who want to kill Americans, but they should pay full price.

However, I don’t think it’s fair to specifically emphasize foreign funding for Israel as like, the main reason Americans can’t afford groceries. We have a trillion-dollar deficit, and spend wildly on all categories of defense, Medicare, and Social Security. That’s the problem.

Maybe that’s why this ad, which was put out by Cenk Uygur’s Rebellion PAC, really rubs me the wrong way. Take a look.

First off, that $26 billion was appropriated by Congress two years ago . President Biden signed off on it. The framing of this ad is that Republicans are going to send every last dollar overseas, but the idea of giving some military aid to Israel is popular and bipartisan. That doesn’t make it right, and I too would object to giving a foreign country more money solely for the purpose of “killing Palestinians.” That, of course, is a ridiculous and pathologically unfair framing. That money is for Israeli security and to support U.S. combat operations against terrorists in the region — terrorists who kill Israelis and want to kill Americans.

New York Times columnist David French called the ad vile . He writes on X:

“One thing that’s so despicable about far-left hatred of Israel is how quickly they just glide past the fact that Israel was subject to horrific terrorist violence. One does not have to agree with all Israeli policies (I certainly don’t) to know that this is a grotesque caricature.

And Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s vanquished primary opponent, wrote on X :

“This type of fearmongering about Israel is wrong. It is not a winning strategy for any state. It does nothing to help Michigan Democrats win up and down the ballot in eight days. Do we need to lower costs by building more homes, securing people’s health care, and creating a fairer federal tax code? Yes, we do!! How we do so is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world. I want to see Democrats succeed at every level, and that means keeping our focus on lowering costs for Michigan families and reining in this out-of-control President.”

Now again, maybe we should spend less money on overseas entanglements, particularly in the Middle East. But this ad is ostensibly in support of El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate for Michigan, and other Democrats.

This idea that if Democrats retake Congress, they are somehow going to run the federal government in a manner that puts more food on your table, that meaningfully lowers the prices of eggs, or anything else, that returns more of your tax dollars to you, is a fantasy. They are proposing the most expansive and expensive agenda in the history of this nation. They are promising to spend much, much more money on health care and education. And they’re actually not claiming that they will meaningfully cut defense spending: What Israel gets is a drop in the bucket.

To be clear, it’s also totally fair to knock Republicans for failing to rein in spending at all. Except for a couple libertarian-leaning principled dissenters like Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, most of the GOP is happy to go along with massive spending that does in fact cause inflation and ultimately hurts the effective amount of your money you get to keep. But at least with the GOP, we get a mostly sane economic policy that contributes to sustained economic growth. I shudder to think what Dems will do when people who share Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warrens’s regulatory priorities get control of Congress.

That’s what is really at stake next week: continued prosperity. So don’t let the far left ragebait you into thinking this is about sending every last egg to Israel.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy stands by terrible Amy Acton ad, but it’s backfiring
articles.summary: Political campaigns are supposed to be tough, but we have to draw a line between challenging an opponent’s record and weaponizing someone’s traumatic childhood.
articles.body:
In the final stretch of Ohio’s race for governor, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is still facing political backlash that turned his campaign’s biggest attack into its biggest liability.

Ramaswamy’s campaign released that now infamous ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar and disputing her allegations of sexual abuse as a child by her stepfather. And even with all the disgust many people have about his campaign stooping this low, Ramaswamy is still firmly standing by the decision .

RAMASWAMY: “The fact of the matter is I am running against somebody who is crazy, unstable and DISHONEST. … If they actually believe these are unfair attacks, you know what my opponent would be doing? She’d be agreeing to show up on a debate with me, as I agreed to on CNN and NBC!”

Acton has responded : “My opponent has chosen to exploit intentionally my childhood to save his struggling campaign but it’s not going to work.”

She’s right. The strategy is not working. Kalshi’s election odds have shifted in Acton’s favor and one of Ohio’s biggest newspapers, the Cleveland Plain Dealer, broke with its policy against endorsing candidates in statewide races to endorse Acton, because of Ramaswamy’s ad.

The newspaper’s editorial board said the ad went too far writing: “A candidate who uses childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it has crossed a line that Ohioans should defend, whatever their party.”

The board added that it could not “remain silent” given the stakes of the election.

Even Ohio’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine, has condemned the ad as “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong.” DeWine, who even endorsed Ramaswamy, urged him to pull it down.

That’s not all the local fallout — several Ohio venues are pulling out of hosting Republican campaign events for Ramaswamy.

According to The New York Times, his campaign has so far declined to back away from the ad and even went a step further in doubling down by recently purchasing more than $4 million in Ohio television airtime to run it.

That’s a significant investment in a strategy that risks keeping voters focused on his judgment instead of the policies he wants to put in place.

And the latest Fox News poll puts Acton ahead , 50 percent to 48 percent, among likely voters.

So, an ad that intended to redirect the campaign away from frustrations over President Trump’s economy and toward questions about Acton’s honesty instead, put Ramaswamy’s own ethics under a microscope for us all to see.

Political campaigns are supposed to be tough, but we have to draw a line between challenging an opponent’s record and weaponizing someone’s traumatic childhood.

It’s not too late — they can still take the ad down and apologize.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Moreno snipes at El-Sayed over ‘used car salesman’ jab at Rogers video

articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) tussled Monday and Tuesday over a campaign advertisement the sitting senator made with the Democrat’s GOP challenger, Rep. Mike Rogers.

Moreno, who was elected in 2024, appeared in a video alongside Rogers posted to the social platform X Monday, pushing for Michiganders to support the GOP candidate.

“Look, Michigan, if you want a senator that wakes up every day caring about you, your family, your economic well-being, that is 100 percent focused on the state of Michigan, not on Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood and all those other things that are on the other side of the globe, this guy, Mike Rogers is going to care about you and your family,” Moreno said in the video.

“This is what this election is about: America and Michigan first, or everybody else first,” he added.

El-Sayed clapped back at Moreno in his own Monday X post, referencing his background in car sales.

“Used car salesman sells used car,” El-Sayed said, appearing to frame Rogers as the “used car.”

Moreno then took his own swipe El-Sayed, saying in a post on X Tuesday, “Yeah, I sold cars.”

The Ohio senator continued, “You sell open borders, higher taxes, government run healthcare, antisemitism, sharia law, and policies that ship auto jobs to China. One of us understands the American Dream. The other wants to kill it. That’s why [Rogers] is going to kick your ass.”

If elected, El-Sayed would be the U.S.’s first Muslim senator. He has faced attacks throughout the midterm election cycle surrounding his background and faith, including attempts to tie him to the Islamist movement, Muslim Brotherhood, and label him a “jihadist.”

El-Sayed has also been critical of U.S. aid to Israel, with the issue of assistance to the country becoming a hot topic among Democrats in the wake of its war in Gaza. While the Democratic Party is split over the military offensive, with some calling the Israeli forces’ actions a genocide, many Republicans have accused Israel’s opponents of antisemitism.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on Moreno’s most recent post.

articles.body:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings says he is concerned about a number of Senate races, highlighting the Texas Senate race among others.

“There are many I’m concerned about. Texas, honestly. It’s got a bad vibe,” Jennings said during a recent appearance on CNN, when asked which Senate race he is most concerned Republicans will lose.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico and GOP opponent Ken Paxton are in a neck-to-neck battle for a Senate seat with nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ narrowly favoring the Democratic nominee. Republicans have long dominated statewide offices in Texas, but this year’s Senate race has been marked as a “toss up.”

“I think Paxton can win,” Jennings added in his remark.

During his appearance, Jennings also said the Senate race in Kansas seemed “concerning” to him.

The state’s incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is facing Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in the growingly competitive race. Earlier this month, election forecasters Sabato’s Crystal Ball and The Cook Political Report shifted state’s Senate race to a “toss-up.”

However, Decision Desk HQ favors Marshall’s bid with a 65 percent probability of him winning the election.

Among the races that concern Jennings, he mentioned “Alaska with the Democrat shenanigans.”

Alaska’s Senate race has been in the headlines owing to disputes over the integrity of state’s elections after the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week claiming the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could give Democrat Mary Peltola an unfair advantage.

Decision Desk HQ leans in favor of Peltola , projecting a 61 percent probability of her winning the election.

“I hate to limit it to one, because there’s a lot of bad vibes out there,” Jennings said during his CNN appearance.

articles.title: Britain's sweeping new crackdown on 'antisocial' behavior sparks free speech backlash: 'Peak insanity'
articles.summary: Shabana Mahmood unveiled respect orders, giving courts power to impose curfews and unlimited fines and ban offenders from town centers in England and Wales.
articles.body: The United Kingdom introduced new "respect orders" across England and Wales on Monday, giving authorities expanded powers to crack down on persistent "antisocial" behavior and drawing criticism from free speech advocates concerned about potential government overreach. The U.K. government’s order enables police and councils to take stronger "enforcement action" against "adult offenders" of persistent "antisocial" behavior, according to a government news release. Under the new restrictions, U.K. courts could ban offenders from town centers or prohibit them from drinking in "public hot spots" like local parks, the announcement states. Courts can impose restrictions and requirements through a civil Respect Order, while individuals who breach an order without a reasonable excuse can face criminal prosecution, including potentially unlimited fines or imprisonment. Under the legislation governing the Respect Orders, antisocial behavior is defined as conduct that has caused, or is likely to cause, harassment, alarm or distress to any person. The definition has prompted concerns from critics that the powers could be applied too broadly, although the law requires judicial approval before an order can be imposed. UK PRIME MINISTER SAYS FOOTBALL FANS 'SINGLED OUT' BY ALCOHOL BAN NOT IMPOSED ON RUGBY MATCHES "Unchecked, antisocial [behavior] blights our communities," Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "But it is not inevitable, and I won’t accept it. For too long, we have lacked the powers we need to deal with this problem properly. From today, that changes: authorities will be able to take tough action against these offenders. "This delivers on a commitment we made to the British people in our manifesto," Mahmood continued. "And, most importantly, those who make life a misery for others will now face the consequences of their actions." Some offenders may be required to "tackle" the "root causes" of their behavior by participating in drug or alcohol treatment or anger-management programs, according to the announcement. Violating a respect order is considered a criminal offense, giving police the power to arrest anyone on charges of violating the rules, according to the press release. Those who defy an order could also face up to two years of jail time. When reached for comment, the U.K. Cabinet Office referred Fox News Digital to the Home Office, which could not immediately be reached for comment. Alan Mendoza, co-founder and executive director of U.K.-based think tank the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital Tuesday that "vague" definitions under the government's respect orders could result in such enforcement actions being wrongfully "applied to lawful speech or protest." "I think the breadth of these orders deserves scrutiny, particularly in the case of potentially unlimited fines," Mendoza explained. "The government has a legitimate duty to tackle genuinely antisocial behaviour, but the powers need to be tightly defined and proportionate. Vague or elastic definitions could allow measures intended for serious nuisance or harassment to be applied to lawful speech or protest. We have already seen similar after all with social media posts and police investigations that follow. "There should be clear statutory limits, proper evidence requirements, judicial oversight and an effective right of appeal," he added. "Online criticism, however unwelcome, should not be treated as antisocial [behavior] simply because it is unpopular or embarrassing to those in authority." UK POLICE APOLOGIZE TO 'FATHER TED' CREATOR GRAHAM LINEHAN FOR ARREST OVER TRANS SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS Mendoza said the U.K. government "should be able to demonstrate that these powers are necessary and contain adequate safeguards against arbitrary or disproportionate use." The orders notably replace civil injunctions for adult offenders and grant U.K. police more enforcement powers, "including the ability to arrest anyone who breaches an order," according to the announcement. The new restrictions have drawn intense criticism across social media, with one X user claiming in a post Monday that the orders are "mental," while another X account referred to the rules as "peak insanity." "Laugh all you want at what a joke England has become, but understand that the U.S. will follow right behind if Democrats ever take full power again," the Federalist CEO and co-founder Sean Davis wrote Monday in an X post. Tech and free speech lawyer Preston Byrne similarly took to social media to criticize the orders, saying that U.K. residents should "keep in mind that one can cause 'harassment, alarm, or distress' in England and Wales by uttering a true statement of fact to someone who doesn't want to hear it, or by offering an honestly-held opinion or belief, spoken or written, which also offends." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP British political commentator Calvin Robinson wrote in an X post Monday responding to the orders that "this tyranny must end." The U.K. has notably enacted a spate of laws restricting free speech in recent years, including the 2023 Online Safety Act, which gives the country's regulator the authority to impose major fines on digital platforms if they fail to comply with certain requirements. The new restrictions come amid growing tensions across Europe, where protests and riots have rocked countries, most notably France.

articles.title: ESPN’s Pat McAfee blasted for comparing himself to Charlie Kirk
articles.summary: ESPN personality Pat McAfee is facing widespread mockery for apparently comparing himself to the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk as he expressed discomfort with the way he was received by students at the University of Utah before a recent trip there for “College GameDay.” McAfee, who is a major player in GameDay’s panel and is…
articles.body:
ESPN personality Pat McAfee is facing widespread mockery for apparently comparing himself to the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk as he expressed discomfort with the way he was received by students at the University of Utah before a recent trip there for “College GameDay.”

McAfee, who is a major player in GameDay’s panel and is known for hyping up the crowds that gather to watch the weekly pregame show, said he “did not enjoy” his trip to Utah.

The pundit said during his daily ESPN show he was unsettled by a post on the university’s Instagram page that featured students talking about the show’s upcoming visit to the school, some of which called him “corny” or “creepy.”

“The university puts that out as I’m about to go out and do an infomercial for this place, this is how the university feels about this,” he said. “It made me feel a little mute … a little bit weird.”

McAfee went a step further, alluding to the assassination of Kirk, which happened on the campus of Utah Valley University.

“I thought to myself, did something else happen pretty scary at a college gathering in the state of Utah recently?” he continued. “Like should we be amplifying reasons why people hate my guts? So I don’t know, it was a lot of mixed feelings.”

The University of Utah later issued an apology for the Instagram post, while McAfee was widely panned on social media for the comparison to Kirk.

“Tough guy can’t handle…critical videos from kids? So he’d last a solid 8, 9 minutes in the real world,” the former cable news pundit Keith Olberman wrote on X, calling him and an “imbecilic child – and soft.”

“Pat McAfee thinking he’s important enough to get assassinated is much funnier than anytime he’s taken his shirt off,” another user wrote on X.

Others argued no apology from the university was necessary.

“They didn’t miss the mark. No apology is needed,” Yahoo Sports columnist Dan Wolken wrote on social media. “Watch the video. This is insanity.”
