articles.title: 2026 midterm elections: When polls close; when results are expected
articles.summary: There are just seven days until the final votes will be cast in the 2026 midterms. Tens of millions of voters across the country have already cast ballots for Senate, House, governor, state legislature and other critical races that will determine the future of President Trump’s agenda. In the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held…
articles.body:
There are just seven days until the final votes will be cast in the 2026 midterms.

Tens of millions of voters across the country have already cast ballots for Senate, House, governor, state legislature and other critical races that will determine the future of President Trump’s agenda.

In the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats to gain control. In the House, Democrats need to pick up just three seats.

One week out, who is winning the race, and when can we expect results in the most anticipated match-ups?

What do the pollsters and forecasters say ?

Public polling has Democrats ahead in more than enough Senate races to take back control, though leads in most states are narrow and within the margin of error.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, gives Democrats a 57 percent chance of Senate control and an 80 percent chance of House control, as of Tuesday afternoon.

For Senate control, Democrats need to win multiple states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Their best pickup opportunity in the Senate is North Carolina, per DDHQ, but the party also leads narrowly in Alaska, Maine, Texas and Ohio. They trail by a small margin in Iowa and are tied in Kansas.

Democrats also lead in the states they are defending: Georgia, Michigan and Minnesota. On a really good night for Democrats, the party would also be eyeing “reach” states where their candidates have some chance of an upset: South Carolina, Mississippi and a Democrat-backed independent candidate in Nebraska.

In the House, Democrats need an even smaller net gain than in the Senate, though Republican redistricting efforts mean the GOP is likely to pick up a few redrawn, deep-red seats. Still, Democrats are comfortably ahead in the race for House control, with Republicans halting spending in key races even as party leadership projects confidence.

DDHQ’s average of the generic congressional ballot, which asks voters which party they plan to vote for in their district, has Democrats ahead by 8.1 points.

Several states have gubernatorial contests, including widely watched races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada and Wisconsin. Democrats have a chance to win a majority of governorships for the first time since 2009.

The first polls in the country close at 6 p.m. ET, and the last polls close at 1 a.m. Some states are split across multiple time zones and will have different poll closing times in different parts of the state.

Polls close at 6 p.m. in parts of Kentucky and Indiana, but the rest of the polls in those states do not close until 7 p.m.

At 7 p.m., polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. Polls close at 7 p.m. in most of Florida and New Hampshire, while the remaining polls close at 8 p.m. At 7:30 p.m., polls close in West Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina.

At 8 p.m., polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. Most polls close at 8 p.m. in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota, with the rest closing at 9 p.m. Polls close at 8:30 p.m. in Arkansas.

At 9 p.m., polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

At 10 p.m., polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls in Idaho close at 10 p.m., with some closing at 11 p.m. Some polls close in the Mountain time zone portion of Oregon at 10 p.m., though most close at 11 p.m. At 11 p.m., polls close in California and Washington.

Polls close in all of Hawaii and in most of Alaska at midnight, with some polls there closing at 1 a.m.

Different states have varying election procedures and thus will count votes at vastly different speeds.

In some states with competitive races, including Florida, North Carolina, Georgia and Texas, votes will be counted relatively quickly. Most votes in those states are cast in person early or on Election Day, and late-arriving mail-in ballots have short windows to arrive after the election.

Some battleground states in the Midwest, namely Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, may take longer than Election Day to count votes. If races in those states are close, they may not be called until the next day. In Michigan, for instance, DDHQ did not call the 2024 presidential race until Thursday afternoon — two days after the election.

States out west tend to conduct elections differently, some almost entirely by mail, with longer windows for ballots to arrive after the election. The most prominent among these is California, where votes are sometimes counted for weeks after the election.

The Golden State has been decisive for House control in the past, including in 2022 and 2024, where a close race meant the nation waited on California to help determine which party would take the majority. A new map drawn to favor Democrats has shrunk the number of competitive House races in the state, which may avoid that scenario this year.

The Hill uses DDHQ projections for most races. DDHQ projects a race when it is 99.9999 percent confident in the result, according to its website.

For federal races, newly elected members are sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, at noon, per the Constitution.

But some congressional elections are technically special elections, meaning the winner will be sworn in sooner.

In Ohio and Florida, both incumbent senators were appointed and are running for their first full term. If Democrats were to win either election, the winner would likely be sworn in before the end of the year, which would immediately reduce the size of the GOP’s majority.

In state and local contests, winners will take office at varying dates depending on state law.

articles.title: Democrats seize on Machado’s return to push for Venezuela elections
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers urged the Venezuelan government to hold elections following opposition leader María Corina Machado’s recent return to the country after nearly a year in exile. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called Machado’s return to Venezuela “welcome news” in a statement shared to social platform X Monday.…
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers urged the Venezuelan government to hold elections following opposition leader María Corina Machado’s recent return to the country after nearly a year in exile.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called Machado’s return to Venezuela “welcome news” in a statement shared to social platform X Monday.

“This is an encouraging step forward,” Shaheen said. “The Trump Administration and the Delcy Rodríguez regime must now ensure her safety and swiftly advance toward elections and a democratic transition.”

Machado, who announced her return Sunday, has pushed for the country to hold elections next year and indicated she would run for the country’s top office. She leads the center-right Vente Venezuela party, countering the ruling United Socialist Party of Venezuela — which has held onto power for almost three decades.

“I will be president when the time comes. But it doesn’t matter. That should be decided in elections by the Venezuelan people,” she said on CBS’s “ Face the Nation ” in February.

President Trump backed Venezuelan Vice President Delcy Rodríguez, a member of the ruling party, to lead the country after his administration captured leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife earlier this year.

Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize last year for her efforts to prove her fellow opposition leader Edmundo González was the verified winner of the country’s 2024 presidential election.

She later presented the award to Trump, who has long coveted this honor, during a meeting at the White House in January.

Trump noted this gift in response to a question from CNN’s Julia Benbrook on Machado’s return from Venezuela, which he was unaware of at the time of the exchange.

“I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman,” he said. “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) heralded Machado’s return as a “moment long awaited by the people of Venezuela” in a Tuesday X post .

“When I met with [Machado], we talked about the importance of a democratic Venezuela, and the need for free and fair elections,” Schumer wrote. “Venezuelans deserve the right to elect their president—there is no time to waste.”

In a Monday post , Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin (Ill.) called the opposition leader’s return “welcome news that should decidedly move the country toward a clear path to free & fair elections next year.”

Republican lawmakers also celebrated Machado’s return and urged Venezuelan leadership to guarantee her safety.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.) called the opposition leader the “legitimate leader of the Venezuelan people” in a Monday X post .

“Her safety & wellbeing is of the utmost importance,” he wrote. “Delcy & Jorge’s pathetic dictatorship will stop at nothing to undermine and intimidate her. They will be held directly responsible for any harm that comes María Corina’s way.”

Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart (R-Fla.) urged in a Sunday evening post that Machado’s “safety must be guaranteed at all times.”

“Today’s event is a sign that the transition process is advancing, and that freedom and democracy in Venezuela are closer than ever,” Díaz-Balart wrote. “The Venezuelan people are not alone.”

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) called Machado’s return a “pivotal moment” for the U.S. and noted Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s efforts under the Trump administration to transition the country into a democracy.

“As Secretary Rubio works toward securing free and fair elections, Maria has returned home,” Scott wrote Monday.

“We are so close to a free, democratic, Venezuela – a nation which acts as a partner to the U.S. and asset to our national and economic security instead of a threat in our own backyard,” he continued. “This is what America First looks like in action.”

articles.title: Zacharia says press corps has ‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’
articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired from her role after five days following a rocky debut and scrutiny of her legal background, accused reporters of fueling “Trump Derangement Syndrome” in their coverage of President Trump. While Zacharia has remained relatively quiet since her ouster less than two weeks ago, in an…
articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired from her role after five days following a rocky debut and scrutiny of her legal background, accused reporters of fueling “Trump Derangement Syndrome” in their coverage of President Trump.

While Zacharia has remained relatively quiet since her ouster less than two weeks ago, in an op-ed published Monday by The New York Post, the former press secretary reiterated her loyalty to the president and blamed the press for her tumultuous coverage.

“The president deserves a press corps that reports his results straight — instead of feeding the incurable Trump Derangement Syndrome that fake news keeps alive,” she wrote.

Zacharia, who returned to California after her firing, made clear she has no plans to abandon Trump, describing her departure from the White House as a temporary setback.

“I’ve always wanted to work for President Donald Trump, so being back in California feels like an interlude — a temporary pause between the work that matters most,” she said.

Zacharia used a quote from Trump’s 1997 book, “The Art of the Comeback,” where he wrote, “Never quit and always hit back.”

The former press secretary said that mantra continued to guide her, adding that she watched the president live by those words on the campaign trail.

Much of the op-ed focused on Trump’s efforts to rally Republican voters ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, where the party is working to protect its Senate and House majorities amid a contentious campaign season.

“He is on the trail because Republican candidates need the turnout boost only he can deliver, and he is supplying it at a pace and intensity the White House has never seen before,” she wrote.

articles.title: Vance responds to question about ‘insulting’ Alaska election lawsuit
articles.summary: Vice President Vance on Tuesday slammed an independent candidate with a similar name to Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as committing “electoral fraud” when answering a question about his administration’s lawsuit over the Senate race in the state. “Why shouldn’t Alaskans find it insulting that the administration appears to be suggesting they can’t read the word…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance on Tuesday slammed an independent candidate with a similar name to Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as committing “electoral fraud” when answering a question about his administration’s lawsuit over the Senate race in the state.

“Why shouldn’t Alaskans find it insulting that the administration appears to be suggesting they can’t read the word ‘incumbent’ on their ballots and know to vote for Senator Sullivan?” a reporter asked Vance on Tuesday.

“Well, I think the question presumes quite a bit. I mean, look, a lot of Alaskans are going to go and look at the ballot and realize exactly what you said, that this is all a big fraud,” the vice president responded.

“But, people are busy. People have lives. People have jobs. And, when you put a person on the ballot explicitly to try to confuse voters, I think that’s the definition of electoral fraud. And I don’t think that we should endorse it,” he added.

Last week, President Trump said he directed the Department of Justice (DOJ) to file a lawsuit to prevent certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses in this year’s midterms.

The DOJ filed the suit last Thursday, stating the existence of a candidate with a name similar to the incumbent Republican senator’s would result in an invalid win for Democrat Mary Peltola. The president told reporters Friday that he had pushed for the election challenge himself.

At the center of the issue is Dan J. Sullivan — a separate candidate — who is running for the upper chamber in Alaska and will appear on the November ballot against Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

The top four vote-receiving candidates in Alaska’s primary go on to the general election. The two Sullivans will show up differently on the ballot, with the senator labeled “incumbent” and “Republican.”

The Hill has reached out to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign for comment.
